column3: Distinguishes prophetic priority, kinship rights, and allied relations rather than collapsing affiliation into descent.
Sets worship of Allah and being among believers against inherited religious alternatives.
Its warning to the hesitant does not clarify Abrahamic affiliation.
Shows the Prophet's believing trust and mercy toward believers.
Frames the surrounding call around shared worship of Allah rather than mutual lordship.
Turning away here adds no clear account of Abrahamic nearness.
Links the Prophet with those who followed him through hardship.
Explicitly rejects inherited labels for Abraham and identifies his directed, non-associating stance.
The repeated warning of what is more fitting is not an affiliation claim.
Directly identifies Allah as the wali of believers and describes that guardianship.
Defines upright orientation as turning the face to the religion without association.
Marks protective allegiance as consequential and bounded, not a neutral label.
Names Allah as guardian and as taking charge of the righteous.
Prevents prophetic authority from becoming lordship and directs learners to the Book.
Sets Allah's guardianship and help over reversing allegiance.
Contrasts hostility and affection by dispositions, not merely by group name.
Complicates blanket group affiliation through differing conduct within the People of the Book.
Makes turning away after a covenant a boundary case for belonging.
Contrasts the final standing of the God-conscious with worldly mockery of believers.
Presents Abraham as grateful, chosen, and guided on a straight path.
Withdrawal only broadly contrasts with the following central to 3:68.
Commands faith in Allah and the Prophet and following him for guidance.
Excludes taking prophets as lords, preserving the direction of worship in the surrounding passage.
Its repeated warning adds no distinct account of nearness to Abraham.
Joins submission to Allah with those who follow the Prophet.
Challenges reserving belief to one's own religious following and locates guidance with Allah.
Treats turning from the true account as a consequential departure, not a competing affiliation.
Shows that kinship can order particular rights without erasing the wider believing community.
Directly joins submission to Allah, good action, and following Abraham's hanif way.
Defines a God-centered side through allegiance to Allah, the Messenger, and believers.
Contrasts mutual protectors among wrongdoers with Allah as wali of the God-conscious.
Denies that wishes or group claims secure a guardian apart from Allah.
Uses priority for suitability to punishment, a distinct and cautionary use of the term.
Its divisive mosque case does not add a clear account of Abrahamic nearness.
Exposes contempt for followers based on social rank.
This withdrawal after service does not clarify the focus relation.
Shows followers of a messenger receiving mercy while later practice remains accountable.
Explicitly commands the Prophet to follow Abraham's hanif way.
Reaffirms Allah as mawla of believers while denying that protection to disbelievers.
Preserves duties of generosity toward kin without making kinship the criterion of nearness.
Defines being hanif for Allah by rejecting association.
Its procedural priority among witnesses is a separate legal use of precedence.
Places Allah's greater claim above partiality toward self, parents, or relatives.
Makes following one straight path the alternative to routes that divide people.
Its conflict instruction does not clarify Abrahamic affiliation.
Places fear of Allah above fear of people, only indirectly relevant to loyal orientation.
Condemns religious fragmentation into parties as contrary to a unified way.
Shows a harmful mawla as a contrary model of entrusted guardianship.
Connects prophetic judgment to the revealed Book, without directly defining Abrahamic nearness.
Refusal to expel believers resists status-based exclusion from the community.
After others turn away, identifies Allah as the believers' sufficient mawla and helper.
The secure city adds no clear element to the focus.
Earlier calling on Allah is only a remote parallel to belonging.
Denies custodial privilege by claim and makes God-conscious practice the criterion for true awliya.
Ranks forms of effort but does not define nearness to Abraham.
Links uncorrupted belief with security and guidance.
States that Allah's awliya are freed from fear and grief.
Household boundaries around the Prophet do not define the affiliation in 3:68.
Adds Abraham's divinely given argument and elevation, not the criterion of nearness.
Makes turning away lead to an inescapably close consequence, a boundary contrast only.
False declarations of lawful and forbidden do not clarify the focus relation.
Shows Abraham maintaining God-given orientation against his people's associating challenge.
Shows that claimed awliya apart from Allah cannot protect from judgment.
Belief in the revealed Book and preserving prayer only broadly support the believer identity.
Adds Abraham's growing certainty through signs of dominion.
Pairs denial and turning away as a contrary directional response.
The announcement of a birth adds no clear element to the focus.
Gives Abraham's own face-turning to the Creator as hanif and non-associating.
Shows protective authority forming through taking Satan as wali and associating.
Denies any wali or helper apart from Allah.
Names Allah the true mawla to whom all return for judgment.
Separates religious ways but does not specify the faithful criterion for Abrahamic nearness.
Connects Allah's guardianship with the repeated deeds that lead to the abode of peace.
Recognition or denial of the blessed reminder does not clarify the focus.
Refuses any wali other than Allah, the Creator and sole provider.
Pairs Allah's sufficiency with the Prophet's believing followers.
Depicts wrongdoers becoming one another's guardians through what they earn.
Limits kinship's claim where the decisive condition has become clear.
Warns that no wali or intercessor exists apart from Allah at gathering.
Defines believers' mutual wilayah through shared corrective, worshipful, and obedient practice.
Names Allah as mawla in a specific oath ruling without developing the focus criterion.
Joins deliverance of messengers with deliverance of believers.
Denies any guardian or intercessor apart from the Creator's authority.
Questions seeking honor through allies other than believers when all honor belongs to Allah.
Shows obedience to hidden satanic allies creating a rival authority and association.
Characterizes the guided as those who listen and follow what is best.
Tests a claimed exclusive nearness to Allah rather than accepting the claim by label.
Makes obedience to Allah and the Messenger the route into the company of the divinely favored.
Limits what any mawla can do for another at judgment.
Defines mutual wilayah through belief, migration, striving, shelter, and help, with stated limits.
Links belief and righteous works to divinely granted affection.
Its confrontation command does not add a clear account of Abrahamic affiliation.
Notes differentiated prophetic rank without identifying the following relation of 3:68.
Universal submission and divine honor provide only a distant backdrop.
Trust, testimony, and God-consciousness are ethical parallels rather than an affiliation account.
Its family maintenance rules do not clarify the focus.
The hearing metaphor does not add a clear element to the focus.
Knowledge of the Hour does not clarify Abrahamic nearness.
Human origin and faculties do not add a clear element to the focus.
Its rejection of association provides only a broad boundary for the focus.
Abraham's tested leadership and the exclusion of wrongdoers make covenantal standing answer to conduct, not descent.
Treats turning from Abraham's millah as self-betrayal and identifies him as surrendered to Allah.
Shows Abraham and Jacob charging their descendants to remain surrendered, linking inheritance to continuing response.
Explicitly answers inherited labels with Abraham's hanif millah and rejection of association.
Places Abraham with the prophets in a shared believing confession rather than a sectarian possession.
Makes following the Prophet the stated condition in a claim of love for Allah.
Joins belief in the revealed message with witnessing submission alongside Jesus's helpers.
Challenges retrospective religious claims over Abraham, directly guarding him from later labels.
Confesses belief in Abraham and all prophets without distinguishing among them.
Directly commands following Abraham's hanif millah and rejects association.
Names Allah as wali of two believing groups at the point of their vulnerability.
Makes disputed allegiance return to Allah and the Messenger through obedience.
Treats obedience to the Messenger as obedience to Allah.
Opposes leaving the Messenger's way and following a way other than that of believers.
Defines believers' wali as Allah, the Messenger, and believers marked by worship and almsgiving.
Forbids taking as awliya those who make religion a mockery, making allegiance a religious boundary.
Links believing in Allah, the Prophet, and revelation with not taking opposing allies.
Commands following the guidance of the prophets, including Abraham in its preceding sequence.
Directly identifies the straight religion with Abraham's hanif millah and non-association.
Commands following what is sent down from the Lord rather than other awliya.
Pairs faith in, support for, and following the unlettered Prophet with success.
Shows mutual protection among disbelievers as a contrasting communal alignment.
Denies protective allegiance to fathers and brothers when they prefer disbelief to faith.
Extends divine approval to the first believing communities and those who follow them with excellence.
Commands believers to remain with the truthful.
Defines Allah's awliya by belief and God-consciousness.
Presents Joseph as following the millah of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob while refusing association.
Shows Abraham seeking protection for himself and his descendants from worshiping idols.
Describes Abraham as a devoted community, hanif, and not among associators.
Introduces Abraham as receiving right guidance before his public struggle against association.
Names Abraham's millah and the community's designation as those surrendered to Allah.
States that obedience to the Messenger is the route to guidance.
Uses those taking awliya other than Allah as a contrary model of fragile reliance.
Links surrendering one's face to Allah with holding the firmest handhold.
Sets the Messenger as an excellent pattern for those oriented to Allah and the Last Day.
Questions claimed awliya besides Allah who are invoked as intermediaries of nearness.
Describes divine guardianship as sustaining believers in this life and the next.
Identifies Allah as wali in contrast to other guardians and grounds that authority in giving life.
Places Abraham within the one religion enjoined through multiple prophets.
Shows Abraham's decisive separation from what his people worshiped.
Makes Abraham's monotheistic declaration an enduring word among his descendants for their return.
Characterizes those with the Messenger by worshipful conduct, mutual mercy, and a distinct communal mark.
Links the Messenger's presence with believers being made to love faith and reject defiance.
Calls believers to fear Allah and believe in His Messenger for mercy and guiding light.
Characterizes the emigrant believers by seeking Allah's favor, supporting Allah and His Messenger, and truthfulness.
Extends belief and prayerful solidarity to earlier believers without rancor.
Forbids making Allah's and believers' enemies into awliya despite prior human ties.
Makes Abraham and those with him a pattern of exclusive worship and separation from association.
Reaffirms Abraham and his companions as a pattern for those hoping in Allah and the Last Day.
Calls believers to be helpers of Allah as Jesus's disciples were.
Pairs obedience to Allah and the Messenger with the Messenger's defined task of clear conveyance.
Contrasts following ancestral custom with following what Allah revealed, directly challenging descent-based allegiance.
Commands obedience to Allah and the Messenger as a concise affiliation criterion.
Commands believers to hold together to Allah's rope and not divide.
Contrasts Satan's allies with fear of Allah by believers.
Describes a people loved by Allah who love Him and stand with believers rather than opponents.
Commands following revealed guidance and leaving awliya apart from Allah.
Addresses believers through obedience to Allah and the Messenger.
Calls believers to answer Allah and the Messenger when summoned to what gives life.
Makes family and kin attachments subordinate to Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His way.
Critiques taking religious authorities as lords alongside Allah.
Makes following guidance one's own benefit and following error one's own loss.
Defines the Prophet's way as calling to Allah with those who follow him.
Makes worship of Allah and avoidance of false powers the message sent to every community.
Commands remaining with those who call on their Lord and rejects status-driven preference.
Makes following Allah's guidance the condition for avoiding error and misery.
Identifies the prophetic community as one community under one Lord and commands God-consciousness.
Contrasts revealed guidance with following desire without guidance from Allah.
Limits obedience to parents where they press association, while preserving worldly kindness.
Repeats the boundary against obeying parents in association while requiring good companionship.
Denies believers an independent choice once Allah and His Messenger decide a matter.
Urges a city to follow the messengers.
Commends those who avoid false powers and turn back to Allah.
Commands steadfastness and a just common call under Allah rather than competing affiliations.
Makes close friends enemies on that Day except the God-conscious.
Commands following the ordained way rather than the desires of those without knowledge.
Links obedience to Allah and the Messenger with preserving one's works.
Names believers brothers and commands reconciliation within that bond.
Makes God-consciousness, not tribal division, the measure of honor before Allah.
Portrays believers as withholding allegiance from opponents of Allah and the Messenger even when they are close kin.
Calls for belief in Allah, His Messenger, and the light sent down.
Places the plea of the oppressed under Allah as protector and helper.
Forbids taking allies from those who turn back from the faith until their position changes.
Forbids believers to seek protective allies among disbelievers instead of believers.
Treats taking rival religious communities as awliya as a consequential alignment.
Describes devils as awliya of those who do not believe.
Addresses Allah as the community's wali and asks for forgiveness and mercy.
Distinguishes those who strive without taking confidants apart from Allah, His Messenger, and believers.
Forbids leaning toward wrongdoers and denies a wali apart from Allah.
Names Allah as Joseph's wali in this life and the next.
Challenges taking awliya other than Allah who cannot control benefit or harm for themselves.
Denies that Allah shares His rule with anyone.
Condemns taking Satan and his offspring as awliya instead of Allah.
Warns against becoming a companion or ally of Satan.
Denies that alleged allies could rightly be taken apart from Allah.
Separates angelic worship from the claimed allegiance of those who followed hidden powers.
Makes Allah's sufficiency the alternative to fear induced by rivals.
Denies any intimate protector or effective intercessor for wrongdoers at judgment.
States that Allah watches over those who take awliya besides Him.
Returns disputed judgment to Allah and places trust in Him.
Warns that refusing Allah's caller leaves no wali apart from Him.
Makes reliance on Allah the response to His exclusive divinity.
Denies refuge or shelter apart from Allah.
